frameworks.name: Front Door Linear Funnel
frameworks.definition: A straight-line offer architecture with three doors (front-end offer, mid-tier, back-end/ascension) where front-end leads become the lead pool for ascension, handled by two or three top closers.

frameworks.name: Prune-Then-Scale Sequence
frameworks.definition: A two-step growth sequence: first eliminate low-margin, low-retention avatars to fix the model; second diagnose and remove what prevents selling 10x more of the single best avatar.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that an organic-content-first business has a natural failure mode: because lead flow comes from a fixed audience pool, founders keep adding product lines to the same pond rather than expanding the pond. The result is a fragmented model with multiple avatars that cannot be served well simultaneously because small teams compete against specialists who focus on each segment as their entire business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Organic content is the primary or only lead-generation channel
Business is at small-to-mid size with limited team bandwidth
claims.mechanism: Organic audiences are finite; adding more product lines is the locally rational response to a fixed lead pool, but it fractures team resources and forces the founder to compete against specialists who do each single thing as their whole business.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the business has a paid acquisition engine that can be expanded independently of audience size

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that when one avatar generates approximately 80% of revenue (as was the case for a door-to-door sales coaching business where owner-clients produced ~80% of revenue vs. ~20% from rep and manager tracks), the correct decision is to eliminate the lower-revenue avatars entirely. The result: roughly 80% of fulfillment complexity is removed while revenue declines by only ~20%, causing margins to increase.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: One avatar segment generates ~80% of revenue
Multiple avatars are being served simultaneously with overlapping team resources
claims.mechanism: Removing the smaller avatars eliminates disproportionate fulfillment cost and management overhead, improving net margin even though top-line revenue falls.
bounded_by: Does not apply when lower-revenue avatars have significantly higher margin or serve as a strategic lead source for the primary avatar

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a service business with a sticky recurring revenue component (in this case $50/user/month SaaS-style training licenses) is fundamentally a better business than one relying solely on one-time program sales, because retention sustains compounding revenue without proportional sales cost.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service business with at least one recurring per-user fee component
claims.mechanism: Sticky recurring revenue means each won customer continues generating revenue without additional CAC, unlike one-time course buyers who exit the revenue base immediately.
bounded_by: Only applies when the recurring component has meaningfully higher retention than the one-time products it is compared against

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that at the ascension layer (high-ticket back-end offers), a business can reach $100 million per year in revenue with only two or three closers, provided the front-end team supplies a qualified customer base and ticket sizes are in the $10,000–$35,000 range.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Front-end offer generates a sufficient volume of qualified buyers
Ascension ticket prices are in the $10,000–$35,000 range
Ascension closers are promoted top performers from the front-end team
claims.mechanism: The customer base from the first sale becomes the qualified lead pool for ascension; because this pool is small relative to cold leads, a small team of high-trust closers can work it without a large headcount.

numbers.axis: Ascension team headcount required to reach $100M revenue

bounded_by: Requires a functioning front-end funnel delivering sufficient qualified buyers
Does not apply to cold-audience ascension without a prior customer relationship

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the correct model for a multi-product business is a straight-line three-door architecture: front-end offer (door one), mid-tier (door two), high-ticket ascension (door three). Once the model is fixed, the only growth question becomes how to increase volume through the front door, not what additional products to add.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has or can have a clear natural ascension path from a front-end entry point
claims.mechanism: A linear funnel concentrates team effort on a single acquisition motion; every additional product line splits management attention and competes for the same team bandwidth.
bounded_by: Does not address businesses where distinct customer segments do not share a natural ascension path

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that for a sales-training business serving door-to-door companies, narrowing the niche to door-to-door broadly (including home services such as pest control, solar, alarms, and roofing) is preferable to further vertical-specific narrowing, because the core sales and recruiting methodology is approximately 80% transferable across door-to-door verticals with only minor sub-module adjustments for financing or product differences.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Service or training business whose methodology is process-driven, not industry-specific
Adjacent verticals share the core customer-acquisition motion (door-knocking, in-home close)
claims.mechanism: Shared core mechanics (door knock, in-home close, commission-based rep management) mean the methodology transfers with minimal adaptation, making a broader niche viable without diluting the value proposition.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the verticals have fundamentally different customer-acquisition motions (e.g., door-to-door vs. digital-only)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that small businesses with limited team bandwidth should focus on a single avatar because they are competing against specialists who do each segment as their entire business. Spreading resources across multiple avatars means the small business will always be outperformed in each segment by a dedicated competitor.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Small business with constrained team bandwidth
Multiple avatar segments each have dedicated specialist competitors
claims.mechanism: Specialists concentrate all resources on one segment and therefore deliver superior product and messaging quality compared to a generalist splitting identical resources across multiple segments.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the business has sufficient scale that separate teams can specialize within the same company

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that unconstrained growth in a business model (adding products, avatars, and revenue lines without pruning) is analogous to cancer: it consumes organizational resources without proportional return and ultimately weakens the core business. Pruning underperforming segments is necessary for the core to grow.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: unconstrained growth is also called cancer
conditions: Business is operating below its resource ceiling and cannot staff each segment adequately
claims.mechanism: Each additional revenue line consumes shared leadership, fulfillment, and sales capacity, reducing the quality and focus applied to the highest-margin segment.
bounded_by: Does not apply at scale where separate teams can own each line independently

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies a two-phase growth sequence for a multi-avatar business that has plateaued: phase one is fixing the model by eliminating low-value avatars; only after the model is fixed does phase two (diagnosing and removing the constraint on selling more to the best avatar) make sense.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business has plateaued (e.g., revenue ceiling) due to model complexity rather than insufficient marketing
claims.mechanism: Diagnosing growth constraints before fixing the model produces misleading answers because the constraint appears to be marketing or sales when the real problem is that the model itself is unfocused.
bounded_by: Does not apply when the model is already focused and the plateau is clearly a demand or execution issue

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that one-time product revenue from lower-tier avatars (e.g., individual sales reps buying a $197–$1,500 course) will exhibit meaningfully lower retention than the recurring per-user licensing fee ($50/user/month) sold to owner-level clients, making the owner avatar the better long-term revenue base.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Comparison between individual contributor (rep/manager) one-time course buyers and owner-tier recurring license buyers
claims.mechanism: One-time course purchases have no structural retention mechanism; per-user recurring licenses tie revenue to ongoing headcount and team activity, creating a natural renewal incentive.

anchors.value: high stickiness (cited as the best business)

examples.text: A door-to-door sales coaching business with three avatars (sales reps, sales managers, and business owners) had plateaued at $7.5M in annual revenue despite targeting $15M. When pressed on revenue breakdown, the founder revealed that owner-clients generated approximately 80% of revenue while reps and managers combined generated only 20%. Alex Hormozi's recommendation: eliminate the rep and manager tracks entirely, accept a ~20% revenue decline, and capture the margin improvement from removing ~80% of fulfillment complexity. The remaining model: front-end boot camp ($2,500), recurring team training license ($6,900 setup + $50/user/month), and a $35,000 mastermind ascension.

The same door-to-door coaching founder had expanded his product suite to include individual sales rep courses ($197 and $1,500), sales manager courses (same price, different content), a business owner boot camp ($2,500), a SaaS-style team training platform ($6,900 + $50/user/month), a mastermind ($35,000), a recruiting service, and a bundled pro package ($15,000 covering both training and recruiting setup). Alex Hormozi diagnosed this proliferation as a classic organic-content trap: the founder built out multiple product lines to monetize a fixed content audience rather than expanding the audience. The fix was to collapse to the owner-avatar funnel only and invest in audience expansion.

On the question of whether the door-to-door sales coaching business should niche strictly to one vertical (e.g., roofing) or remain broad across door-to-door and home services, Alex Hormozi framed the positioning test as: if a solar company owner and a pest control company owner are both in the room, can you say something that resonates with both? His answer was yes, because the core question both face is: do your reps knock on doors and close people in their homes? That shared motion makes the methodology transferable, with vertical-specific financing or product differences handled as sub-modules rather than separate offers.

practices.text: When diagnosing a revenue plateau, identify which avatar generates the largest share of revenue before deciding whether to add products or cut avatars.
After identifying the highest-value avatar, promote the one or two best front-end sales reps to handle back-end ascension exclusively rather than hiring new ascension closers.

For a niche selection decision between two adjacent verticals, test whether a single positioning statement covering both resonates with buyers from each vertical before deciding to split or combine them.
Once the model is simplified to a single avatar and linear funnel, shift all strategic energy to the question of what is preventing 10x more of the best avatar from entering the front door.
